title: Question unusual related-party dealings
full_text:
SMSF auditors need to question the validity of any arrangement where a fund rents a commercial property to a related party and the actions between the entities appear irregular or specific to the two of them, two audit specialists have stated.
Auditors Institute ambassador Graeme Colley highlighted a common arrangement in which an SMSF leased a commercial property to a related party, but created questions about that arrangement when nine months’ rent, worth $450,000, was paid upfront to secure the lease.
“This is an interesting case to work out whether the transaction is actually on an arm’s-length basis,” Colley said during a webinar presented by the institute today.
“There are probably some tax consequences in paying the $450,000 upfront, as well as whether this could be regarded as arm’s length because why would a related party need to secure the lease unless it was in competition with other people.”
Auditors Institute director and Assurify managing director David Burrows added these types of arrangements and their underlying nature were key areas of concern for auditors, given it was easy for things to go wrong with related-party rental arrangements.
“There can be commercial or tax reasons why someone might want to prepay rent in advance, but from my perspective we would generally accept that as being arm’s length because tax is a viable consideration,” Burrows stated.
“I would question what an arm’s-length party might get in the same circumstances if they asked the landlord for a discount for upfront payment and, in this case in particular, to secure the lease, that seems a little bit strange and I would want to know more about that.”
Colley added if the related party was competing with a non-related party that was also prepared to pay rent in advance, it was more likely the arrangement was at arm’s-length, but Burrows emphasised auditors still needed to be asking for evidence to demonstrate that was the case.
“If you have an SMSF that owns a property and the plan is for a related party to rent that property, I can’t imagine it has gone to market to get an offer from an arm’s-length party to prepay the rent,” he said.
“So, definitely, this is the type of area where auditors will spend their time and it is the responsibility of the trustee to demonstrate they are acting on an arm’s-length basis.
“Auditors need to keep pushing back asking: ‘Where is the evidence?’ We don’t need to provide all the solutions, but need to ask the right questions.”
author: Jason Spits
